entry.title: idemkit: make any Python operation safe to retry (HTTP, queues, functions)
entry.summary: A few years ago, I spent about a month cleaning up duplicate charges. Every service involved already had idempotency "handled": the client sends an Idempotency-Key header, we store the response under it, and if the key comes back we replay the stored response. Textbook. And it still double-charged people. What finally clicked for me is that the key is just a name for the request. It doesn't do anything on its own. Whatever safety you have comes from the code around it, and that code is a small distributed state machine that's easy to get wrong. A few of the ways it went wrong for us: Two requests with the same key arrive a millisecond apart. Both read "no record yet," both write one, both run. A check-then-act race. The fix is to make the write itself the check, one atomic insert, so exact…

entry.title: Building SaarDB, Part 4: Transactions
entry.summary:
In Parts 1-3, we built a storage engine: WAL, memtable, SSTables, and compaction. Every operation is a single GET or PUT. But real applications rarely need just one write at a time. Consider a bank transfer: move $100 from account A to account B. PUT account_A 400 (was 500, debit 100) PUT account_B 600 (was 500, credit 100)
Now imagine the process crashes between these two writes. The first PUT succeeds, account A has $400. The second PUT never happens, account B still has $500. $100 has vanished. The system is in an inconsistent state. In our current system, each PUT is independent. There is no way to say: "these two writes must both succeed or both fail." This is the atomicity problem. entry.title: Pepper Remastered coming soon
entry.summary:
I've decided to create a more feature-rich version of Pepper, an experimental virtual VR device that allows you to use SteamVR without requiring a physical VR headset or controllers. Using only a keyboard and mouse, Pepper creates a fake VR device that SteamVR recognizes, allowing you to play supported VR games from your Steam library. The original Pepper that I made a few months ago was a small proof-of-concept showing that it was possible to create a software-only VR device using SteamVR's driver system. While it worked, it was limited and required a lot of manual setup. Pepper Remastered aims to rebuild the project with a stronger foundation, better usability, and more features. What is changing in Pepper?
Full rewrite of the Pepper VR driver architecture Support for a more realistic virtual HMD and controller system Improved SteamVR compatibility and stability New Pepper control center for managing settings and devices Advanced keyboard and mouse VR controls Custom controller mapping and input profiles Support for gamepads as virtual VR controllers Improved virtual tracking and movement system Adjustable movement speed, sensitivity, and smoothing Better driver performance and reduced latency Automatic SteamVR driver installation Easier setup process for new users Improved error reporting and debugging tools Real-time tracking and device monitoring Modular system for adding new input methods Virtual device profiles and configuration support Better support for experimental VR setups Foundation for future OpenXR support Alongside the PC version, I have also been experimenting with mobile support. You can follow the development of Pepper Remastered through my GitHub profile: https://github.com/blakebeckcoding

entry.title: Webhook Retries Aren't Optional: The 6-Hour Silent Failure That Changed How We Build Them
entry.summary: We found out our webhook delivery was broken the same way most teams do: a customer told us. Not an alert, not a dashboard going red — an email asking why a payment status update from three hours earlier had never shown up in their system. By the time we'd pulled the logs, we counted just over six hours where a downstream endpoint had been failing silently, and every event meant for it was gone. Not queued, not retried. Gone. The endpoint in question belonged to a mid-sized integration partner whose ops team had rotated a TLS cert and, in the process, briefly served a handshake our client library didn't like.
